Interactive Brokers vs Robinhood — how each makes money

IBKR-vs-HOOD-2026-10-09 · USD · series 2026-10-09T02:00:00Z · built 2026-10-09 02:06 UTC

The short version

Both firms run a brokerage on their own technology and both earn the same two kinds of money: a cut of each trade, and the spread on client cash and margin loans. They sell to very different customers. Interactive Brokers serves active traders, advisers and institutions in over 200 countries and territories, and charges a commission. Robinhood serves U.S. retail investors through an app with no commission, and is paid mostly by the market makers who fill its customers' orders (payment for order flow, or PFOF). That difference shows up in every chart below. Interactive Brokers earns about nine times more revenue per account and keeps 77 cents of each revenue dollar as pre-tax profit. Robinhood is smaller, faster growing and more tied to options and crypto trading. Both lose about the same share of revenue when rates fall.

Where the money comes from

Net interest income (NII) is interest earned on client cash, margin loans and the firm's own investments, less the interest paid out. It is the larger stream at Interactive Brokers and has grown from about two-fifths to more than half of revenue since 2016. At Robinhood, trading revenue leads, and options and crypto make up most of it.

Open gaps

  • Robinhood has no audited annual figures before 2019, so 2016 to 2018 stay blank on every chart.
  • Interactive Brokers does not print a quarter-point interest sensitivity for 2016 or 2017, and prints only the U.S. dollar figure for 2018 to 2021.
  • Interactive Brokers counts accounts; Robinhood counts unique funded customers. Read the per-account gap as a scale, not an exact multiple.
  • Interactive Brokers does not report crypto revenue or Robinhood-style subscription revenue as separate lines.
